passages.happening:
David reviews his troops and sends them out in three divisions, under Joab, Abishai and Ittai the Gittite. He means to march with them. But the people plead with him to stay: “You must not go out! For if we have to flee, they will pay no attention to us. Even if half of us die, they will not care; but you are worth ten thousand of us” (verse 3). So he stands beside the gate as the troops march out.

The king gives an order to Joab, Abishai and Ittai: “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake” (verse 5). All the people hear it.

The battle is fought in the forest of Ephraim, and Israel is beaten by David's men. The fighting spreads over the whole countryside, ‘and that day the forest devoured more people than the sword’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The revolt that began with a son stealing Israel's heart ends with that son's death. David's throne is saved, at the cost of the son he loved.

Kings often led their armies in person. The people's plea that David stay behind reflects the fact that the war was about him. If he fell, the revolt would win.

David's order is unusual and tender. The word for gently is rare. He calls Absalom the young man, the way a father speaks of a son he still sees as a boy, even when that son is trying to take his throne. And the narrator makes sure the reader knows that everyone heard the order.

The forest of Ephraim lay where the armies met. Since David was at Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, and Absalom had crossed into Gilead, most scholars place this forest in Gilead rather than in Ephraim's land west of the river, though the reason for the name is unclear. Rough, wooded ground explains why the forest devoured more than the sword: broken ground, thickets and pits could destroy a fleeing army.
passages.later: Psalm 3, headed for this flight, prays for rescue from the revolt and ends, ‘Salvation belongs to the LORD’ (Psalm 3:8). The notes on that psalm observe that a man can pray for rescue from a violent rebellion and still love the one who leads it.
passages.asks: David asked his commanders to deal gently with the son who was trying to kill him. Ask whom you still love who has done you real harm. And ask what it would look like to want their good without pretending the harm away.

passages.happening:
Absalom, riding his mule, meets David's men. As the mule passes under the thick branches of a large oak, Absalom's head is caught fast in the tree, and the mule goes on from under him, leaving him hanging in midair (verse 9).

A man tells Joab what he has seen. Joab asks why he did not kill Absalom, and says he would have paid him for it. The man answers that not even for a thousand shekels would he lift his hand against the king's son, ‘For we heard the king command you and Abishai and Ittai’ (verse 12). Joab will not wait. He takes three spears and drives them into Absalom while he is still hanging alive in the oak, and ten of Joab's armor-bearers surround him and kill him (verses 14-15).

Joab blows the ram's horn, and the troops stop pursuing Israel. They throw Absalom into a large pit in the forest and pile a great heap of stones over him (verses 16-17). In his lifetime Absalom had set up a pillar for himself in the King's Valley, saying, “I have no son to preserve the memory of my name” (verse 18). It was still called Absalom's Monument when the book was written.
passages.hearers:
Absalom's mule was a royal mount. Losing it as it passes from under him is a picture of losing the kingdom. Absalom's head is caught in the tree, and the proud prince is left hanging between earth and sky.

The soldier who refuses to kill him is shown as the one who respected the king. He knows the order, and he knows Joab would not stand behind him if the king learned of it. Joab, as at Abner's death, removes a threat by his own judgment.

The burial is a shameful one. A pit in the forest under a heap of stones recalls the burials of Achan and of the king of Ai, both judged men. Absalom, who had built himself a monument, ends under a pile of rocks. His words about having no son sit uneasily beside 14:27, which names three sons; many think they died young. The King's Valley was probably near Jerusalem. The striking tomb in the Kidron Valley that visitors know today as Absalom's Tomb dates from the Roman period, about a thousand years after him, and it is not the pillar this verse describes.
passages.later:
The heap of stones recalls the stones over Achan, ‘a large pile of rocks that remains to this day’ (Joshua 7:26), and over the king of Ai, over whom ‘they raised a large pile of rocks’ (Joshua 8:29).

The King's Valley is named in Abram's day, when the king of Sodom met him ‘in the Valley of Shaveh (that is, the King’s Valley)’ (Genesis 14:17).
passages.hard:
Was Joab right to kill Absalom against David's command?

Opinions divide. Some see Joab as a hard but realistic soldier. As long as Absalom lived, the revolt would go on, and David's feelings were putting the kingdom in danger. On this reading Joab did what the king should have wanted.

Others see Joab as a law to himself. He disobeyed a direct royal order given in everyone's hearing, and he had already murdered Abner and would later murder Amasa, always removing rivals and threats by his own judgment. David did not forget, and near his death he asked Solomon to deal with Joab.

The narrator tells the killing without approval, and the soldier who refused is the one shown honoring the king. The chapter leaves the reader with the tension between a father's mercy and the demands of justice and order.
passages.asks: The soldier would not kill the king's son for any reward. Ask what you would refuse to do even if you were sure no one would ever find out. And ask whose orders you would set aside if you were certain you knew better.

passages.t: Two runners, and a father's cry
passages.happening:
Ahimaaz, the son of Zadok, wants to run to the king with the good news. Joab refuses him: ‘You are not the man to take good news today’ (verse 20), because the king's son is dead. He sends a Cushite instead. But Ahimaaz begs to run too, and he goes by the plain and outruns the Cushite.

David is sitting between the two gates. The watchman sees a man running alone, and then another. “If he is alone,” the king replied, “he bears good news” (verse 25). Ahimaaz arrives first and calls out, “All is well!” (verse 28), and tells of the victory. The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom all right?” (verse 29). Ahimaaz says he saw a great tumult but does not know what it was.

Then the Cushite comes with the news of the victory. The king asks him the same question, and the Cushite answers, “May what has become of the young man happen to the enemies of my lord the king and to all who rise up against you to harm you” (verse 32).

The king is shaken. He goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, and as he walks he cries out, “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
News traveled by runners. A single runner usually meant a messenger, while a crowd running meant a rout, which is why David reasons that a lone runner brings good news. Good news of victory was expected to bring the messenger a reward, and Joab doubts that Ahimaaz will get one when the news includes the death of the king's son.

The scene is full of dramatic irony. The reader knows Absalom is dead, and David does not. Ahimaaz arrives first and avoids the question. The Cushite arrives second and answers it without saying it. David's question is the same both times, and word for word it asks whether there is peace, shalom, for the young man. There is no peace for the king's son.

The chapter is framed by David at the gate, sending the troops out and waiting for news. The battle is told briefly. The narrator slows down for Absalom's death and for the runners, and the chapter ends with a lament in which the word son comes five times. The victory that saved David's throne cost him the son he loved. Nathan's word that the sword would never leave his house has now taken a third son: the infant, Amnon, and Absalom.
passages.later: Joseph's father grieved like this when he thought his son was dead: ‘I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son’ (Genesis 37:35).
passages.hard:
How can David grieve so deeply for a son who tried to kill him?

David's lament shows a father's love that survived betrayal. It also exposes his earlier failures. He loved Absalom but never confronted him, and the love that could not discipline can now only mourn. Absalom's revolt ends in shame and death, and the chapter does not rejoice. Even a judgment that was deserved is no cause for gloating when it falls on a son.

His cry, ‘If only I had died instead of you’, is the wish of a father who would trade places with the one he lost. Victory and loss have arrived together, and the Bible lets him grieve.

If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, or you feel you do not want to go on, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. You do not have to carry it alone. If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The same news was victory for the army and ruin for the king. Ask how you hold together a good outcome and a real loss. And ask whether there is someone you love whom you avoided confronting, and what love might still do while there is time.
